think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 25-year-old postpartum female presents on day 43 following an emergency cesarean section with high fevers, altered mental status, and a 6x7 cm cystic right adnexal mass (tubo-ovarian abscess). She initially had transient symptomatic improvement with a 7-day course of ceftazidime followed by acute relapse upon cessation. The tension lies in diagnosing Burkholderia pseudomallei as the etiologic pathogen of puerperal pelvic abscess and sepsis—an exceedingly rare and lethal tropical presentation—distinguishing it from common polymicrobial puerperal infections and pelvic tuberculosis, and recognizing that melioidosis requires prolonged intensive and eradication antimicrobial therapy rather than standard short-course empiric regimens.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical presentation concludes following the physical examination, pelvic exam, initial triage labs (Hb 9.2 g/dL, WBC 17,000/μL with neutrophilic predominance, platelets 200,000/μL), and pelvic CECT showing the multiseptated cystic right adnexal lesion, prior to emergency exploratory laparotomy, surgical pus drainage, and microbiological cultures.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pelvic tuberculosis can present subacutely with a multiseptated adnexal mass, fever, and constitutional decline in endemic areas, but was excluded by negative CBNAAT testing of intraoperative pus. Typical polymicrobial puerperal pelvic infection (anaerobes, enteric Gram-negative bacilli, Streptococcus spp.) is the leading cause of postpartum tubo-ovarian abscess, but standard empiric therapies do not provide definitive clearance, and specific culture isolation of bipolar-staining non-lactose fermenting bacilli confirmed Burkholderia pseudomallei.
case_prompt: A 25-year-old female (gravida 2, para 1, aborta 1) presents to the emergency department on postpartum day 43 with intermittent high-grade fevers and progressive deterioration. She had undergone an emergency lower-segment cesarean delivery at 35 weeks of gestation due to severe oligohydramnios and intrauterine growth restriction, following an otherwise uneventful antenatal course. Intermittent fevers began on postoperative day 1. She was initially treated at an outside hospital with a 7-day course of intravenous ceftazidime, resulting in transient improvement. However, shortly after completion of antibiotics, she developed a recurrence of high fever associated with vomiting and altered sensorium. She reports no dysuria, night sweats, or cough. On physical examination, she is conscious and follows commands but is disoriented with incoherent speech. Pallor and mild bilateral pitting pedal edema are noted, without icterus, cyanosis, or lymphadenopathy. Vital signs reveal a temperature of 38.4°C (101.2°F), pulse rate of 138 beats/min, blood pressure of 108/66 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 30 breaths/min with oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. The surgical scar is well-healed. Abdominal examination demonstrates mild tenderness in the right hypochondrium with localized guarding, with no palpable organomegaly. On pelvic examination, speculum inspection reveals greenish cervical discharge. Bimanual examination demonstrates a mobile, anteverted uterus (8–10 weeks size) and a 6 × 7 cm cystic, non-tender right adnexal mass displacing the cervix to the left. Initial laboratory testing reveals a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, total leukocyte count of 17,000/μL with neutrophilic predominance, and platelet count of 200,000/μL. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrates a 5 × 4 cm multiseptated cystic lesion in the right adnexa with no solid component and a normal-sized uterus without intrauterine collection.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Pelvic tuberculosis was considered due to the subacute presentation of a multiseptated pelvic mass with systemic inflammatory signs in an endemic region, but molecular testing for mycobacterial DNA on pus was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: CBNAAT for   M. tuberculosis   complex was negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Polymicrobial puerperal pelvic inflammatory disease / Tubo-ovarian abscess
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Common puerperal pelvic pathogens (enteric Gram-negatives, anaerobes, Streptococci) cause postpartum abscesses, but do not explain the rapid relapse after initial ceftazidime therapy or the specific microbiological features of non-lactose fermenting colonies with a metallic sheen.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: On MacConkey agar, non-lactose-fermenting colonies with a metallic sheen were seen (Fig. 2). Gram staining from the colonies revealed Gram-negative bacilli with bipolar staining (Fig. 3) which were catalase-positive and oxidase-positive.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Tubo-ovarian abscess due to Burkholderia pseudomallei (Melioidosis)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic turning point was the microbiological isolation and automated identification of Burkholderia pseudomallei from intraoperative pus, peripheral blood cultures, and high vaginal swab, confirming disseminated melioidosis presenting as puerperal pelvic sepsis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Colonies were subjected to identification by Vitek 2 (bioMerieux, France) and identified as   B. pseudomallei   which was found to be sensitive to ceftazidime, meropenem and co-trimoxazole.

editor_comments: Distilled in strict adherence to the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Zero spoilers or pathogen names in the clinical presentation. Verbatim quotes from the published report support each differential diagnosis and diagnostic pivot.
